name: Documentary deep dive (TV-paced)
summary: A researched, cinematic 25-60 minute story about one company, person, event or scandal, built to be watched on a TV.

structure.what: Drop into the most dramatic moment of the story, then cut to title.
State the central question the film answers and why it matters now.
Backstory with archive footage, maps, documents and interviews.
Turning points and reversals; a mid-film reveal around the halfway mark.
Consequences, what happened to the people, the present day.
What it means; tease the next episode or a related film.

hookTemplates: On [date], [person] made a decision that would cost [number] people everything.
This is the story of how [thing] went from [peak] to [ruin] in [timeframe].
thumbnailPattern: One iconic subject photo or object, high contrast, two to four words or none, readable from ten feet away.
retentionTips: Slower pacing is fine on TV but each act must open a new question.
Invest in clean audio; TV viewers notice it.
Use chapters so living-room viewers can resume.
Plant the mid-film reveal before minute 15.
trendNote: Over half of US YouTube watch time is on TV; Paddy Galloway says TV rewards 20+ minute, slower, higher-production videos in 2026, and average long-form length is up 51% since 2020. PBS launched a dedicated documentaries channel on YouTube in March 2026.
riskNote: Low if you write and voice it; footage-heavy faceless versions with TTS fall into the inauthentic bucket.

name: True crime case narration
summary: One case told chronologically, from the first call to the verdict, with evidence and interrogation footage.

structure.what: The most unsettling detail of the case, out of order.
Who the victim and suspect were; place and date.
Evidence, timelines, bodycam or interrogation clips with analysis.
The detail that changed the case.

hookTemplates: The 911 call lasted [N] seconds. What the caller didn't say is what solved it.
Detectives had one piece of evidence. It was enough.
thumbnailPattern: Suspect or location photo with one red-circled detail and a three-word caption.
retentionTips: Reveal the timeline in layers rather than all at once.
Add analysis between footage segments, not just narration.
Avoid sensational shock framing, which the 2026 'off-putting content' category targets.
trendNote: True crime is among the fastest-growing niches by subscriber growth rate (1.34% in a 30-day window to Oct 2026, per AIR Media-Tech) but is a mature, crowded format.
riskNote: Graphic content gets limited ads; reused bodycam with thin narration risks reused-content review.

examples.note: on-camera storyteller format for strange, dark and mysterious cases

name: Revenge and betrayal story narration (long)
summary: A 20-60 minute narrated first-person family or workplace betrayal story with a satisfying comeuppance.

structure.what: The betrayal in one line ('My son sold my house while I was in hospital').
Who the narrator is, what they built, who the antagonist is.
Three or four rising insults or schemes.
The narrator discovers leverage: a document, a will, a recording.
Public comeuppance, then a quiet closing reflection.

titlePatterns: They Laughed When I [Action]. Then the Lawyer Read the Will.
hookTemplates: The day after the funeral, my daughter-in-law changed the locks.
They thought I didn't know about the second account.
thumbnailPattern: A stock or illustrated older narrator with a shocked antagonist, plus one quoted line of dialogue.
retentionTips: Write original stories, not lightly reworded Reddit posts.
Give the narrator a recurring voice and persona across episodes.
Escalate every 3-5 minutes.
trendNote: OutlierKit tracks betrayal/revenge storytelling at 21x year-over-year growth, and its September 2026 drama report lists AI-narrated revenge stories as one of the four fastest-growing drama sub-niches, aimed at US adults 25-54.
riskNote: This is the exact 'templated storylines' pattern that YouTube's July 2026 clarification names; a channel full of interchangeable TTS stories is likely to be demonetized.

examples.note: on-camera reading and reacting to family-drama stories, which counts as transformative
curated Reddit drama with human editorial voice

name: Analog horror and found-footage web series
summary: A serialized fictional horror world told through fake archival tapes, building lore across episodes.

structure.what: Static, timestamp, an innocuous scene that is slightly wrong.
The 'found' tape or broadcast plays out in real time.
The anomaly appears; the camera keeps rolling.
A clue that connects to earlier episodes.

hookTemplates: (No spoken hook: a timestamp and an empty corridor)
This tape was recovered from [place] in [year].
thumbnailPattern: A grainy VHS frame of a liminal space with a tiny wrong detail, no text.
retentionTips: Hide clues for commenters to decode; lore drives rewatches.
Keep episodes short and frequent; the series is the product.
Use Shorts series or playlists so viewers binge in order.
trendNote: Kane Parsons' YouTube Backrooms series became the A24 film Backrooms (May 2026), A24's highest-grossing film at about $402M; YouTube's September 2026 Culture & Trends report uses it as the model for niche-to-mainstream.
riskNote: Original fiction; only risk is age-restriction on gore.

name: Creator TV show in seasons
summary: A recurring branded show with a fixed premise, host and guests, released as numbered episodes and seasons like TV.

structure.what: Best moment of the episode as a teaser.
Show open, recurring intro and today's guest or mission.
Signature ending ritual; next episode tease.

titlePatterns: I Tried [Job] for a Week | [Show Name]
hookTemplates: Welcome back to [Show]. Today [guest] has [constraint].
Season [N], episode [N]: this one went wrong fast.
thumbnailPattern: Host plus guest in the show's fixed visual frame, with the show logo in the same corner every time.
retentionTips: Keep a fixed segment order so returning viewers know what is coming.
Use the Creator Shows / seasons tooling so TV viewers get sequential playback.
Guests bring audiences; tag them with Collabs.
trendNote: YouTube's trends reporting cites Quenlin Blackwell's 'Feeding Starving Celebrities' growing from 10-minute slots to hour-long episodes; TechCrunch notes Michelle Khare and Rhett & Link using Creator Shows seasons (Sept 2026).
riskNote: Fully original, on camera.

examples.note: daily talk/game show with fixed segments

name: A day in the life of a [historical person]
summary: An hour-by-hour walk through an ordinary person's day in another era: food, work, hygiene and danger.

structure.what: A visceral detail ('You wake at 4am on a straw mattress full of lice').
Disease, law, violence: the part people remember.
Would you survive? Prompt for comments.

titlePatterns: A Day in the Life of a [Role] in [Era]
What It Was Like to Be a [Role] in [Place]
Would You Survive a Day as a [Role]?
hookTemplates: Congratulations, you were just born a [role] in [year]. Here's your day.
By sunrise, a [role] had already done more work than you do all week.
thumbnailPattern: An illustrated or AI-assisted figure in period costume with one gross or dangerous object highlighted.
retentionTips: Use second person ('you') throughout.
Cite sources on screen; AI history visuals are drawing accuracy criticism.
Close each section with a cliffhanger fact.
trendNote: Evergreen long-form; its Shorts cousin (AI time-traveller POV) exploded in 2025-26, feeding interest back to long versions.
riskNote: AI stills plus TTS in a fixed template invites 'generic or repetitive' review; original research and voice keep it safe.

examples.note: animated 'day in the life' and what-if episodes

name: Video essay
summary: An argued, personal analysis of a film, game, trend or idea, with a thesis the viewer can disagree with.

structure.what: A provocative claim or a specific scene.
What this essay argues and why it matters.
Three to five chapters, each a mini-argument with clips.
Restate the thesis with a new emotional beat.

hookTemplates: There's a scene in [work] that explains everything wrong with [industry].
Everyone says [common belief]. I think the opposite is true.
thumbnailPattern: A single well-known image with an odd edit or a short bold claim in two to three words.
retentionTips: Use chapters; long essays are watched in sessions on TV.
Keep commentary-to-clip ratio high for fair use and reused-content safety.
Each chapter should end on a question.
trendNote: Videos 15+ minutes make up a small share of uploads but a large share of engagement, and TV viewing favors them; the format is mature rather than surging.
riskNote: Transformative by design; risk only from Content ID on long clips.

name: What happens if / What if
summary: A hypothetical scenario followed step by step through its consequences, from minute one to centuries later.

structure.what: State the hypothetical with one vivid image.
Cascading consequences for people and systems.
Centuries later; what it says about our world now.

hookTemplates: In the next 60 seconds, every [thing] on Earth vanishes. Here's what happens.
If you [action], your body has about [N] seconds.
thumbnailPattern: Familiar object or planet in an impossible state, with a short question.
retentionTips: Use a visible timeline counter so viewers know how far in they are.
Each step should be more surprising than the last.
Cut a 60-90 s Shorts version of the most shocking step.
trendNote: Evergreen curiosity format; Shorts versions benefit from 90-second dense-narrative Shorts doing well.
riskNote: Easy to template with AI; vary visuals and research per episode.

name: Iceberg explained
summary: A tier-by-tier descent through an iceberg chart, from known facts at the top to the most obscure at the bottom.

structure.what: Show the full iceberg and tease the darkest entry.
Obscure or unverified entries, with caveats.

hookTemplates: Everyone knows the top of this iceberg. Almost nobody has heard of the bottom.
Tier one is trivia. Tier seven is why this video is age-restricted.
thumbnailPattern: The iceberg graphic with a glowing or redacted bottom tier.
retentionTips: Show your position on the iceberg at all times.
Use chapters per tier for TV viewers.
Debunk where needed, which builds trust and avoids misinformation strikes.
trendNote: Long-running format; 2026 uploads like a four-hour conspiracy iceberg still pull views, and multi-hour runtimes suit TV.
riskNote: Original commentary; watch for misinformation policies on conspiracy topics.

name: Explaining X in N levels of difficulty
summary: An expert explains one concept to a child, a teen, a student, a grad student and a peer.
titlePatterns: I Explained [Concept] to a 5-Year-Old and a PhD
hookTemplates: I'm going to explain [concept] five times, each harder than the last.
Level one is a kid. Level five has a Nobel nomination.
thumbnailPattern: Split frame of the expert and a child, numbered level badges.
retentionTips: Viewers drop in at their level, so chapter each level.
Cast real people; chemistry carries it.
Clip level 1 as a Short.
trendNote: Long-running WIRED franchise (about 25 min average); widely adapted by smaller educators.
riskNote: Original, on camera.

name: Map animation history
summary: Borders, empires and wars animated year by year on a map, narrated or set to music.

structure.what: Start map with a question ('How did a tiny state become an empire?').
The world or region at year zero.
Year counter running; key battles zoomed.

hookTemplates: In [year], [country] didn't exist. Watch.
This map changes [N] times in the next ten minutes.
thumbnailPattern: A colored map with an arrow and one bold year.
retentionTips: Keep a year counter on screen.
Zoom into battles; static maps lose viewers.
Vertical cuts of single wars work as Shorts.
trendNote: Long-established 'every year' format; history is one of the dense-narrative niches where longer Shorts now perform.
riskNote: Fine with original maps and narration; music-only repetitive uploads risk repetitive-content review.

name: Animated science explainer
summary: A beautifully animated, tightly scripted answer to one big science or philosophy question.

structure.what: A simple question with a surprising answer.

hookTemplates: Right now, [N] [things] are passing through your body.
This is the most [adjective] thing we know about.
thumbnailPattern: A signature illustration style with a single central object.
retentionTips: A consistent art style is your brand.
Use dubbing; animation travels across languages (half of animation fans watch outside their own language).
Fact-check in description; trust is the moat.
trendNote: YouTube's April 2026 animation report: 61% of Gen Z animation fans prefer independent YouTube animation equally or more than studio work, and 50% watch in other languages, which suits auto-dubbing.
riskNote: Original animation and scripts.

name: Lore and fan theory explained
summary: The full timeline or a bold theory about a game, show or meme universe, built from in-world clues.

structure.what: What would prove it wrong; ask comments.

hookTemplates: There's a frame in [episode] that changes how you see the whole series.
You've been reading [character] wrong.
thumbnailPattern: Character face with a red circle on a tiny background detail.
retentionTips: Lore fans rewatch; reward them with hidden callbacks.
Fan participation is how niche properties go mainstream, so invite theories.
Make Shorts of single clues.
trendNote: YouTube's Sept 2026 'In Search of Mainstream' report centers fan lore (Backrooms) and Italian brainrot as participation-driven culture; 'explained' videos of brainrot characters have spread.
riskNote: Commentary is transformative; keep clips short.

name: Legal and courtroom commentary
summary: A lawyer or legal analyst breaks down a trial, lawsuit or viral legal moment and predicts the outcome.

structure.what: The moment from court everyone is sharing.
What the law says will happen.
What to watch next; live stream invite.

titlePatterns: Why [Celebrity] Is Going to Lose This Lawsuit
hookTemplates: In one sentence, [witness] just blew up the defense.
This lawsuit is weaker than the headlines say. Here's why.
thumbnailPattern: Host plus the defendant, a legal document graphic and a verdict word.
retentionTips: Credentials on screen early.
Pair with live trial watch-alongs.
Clip the single best legal insight as a Short.
trendNote: OutlierKit's Sept 2026 drama report lists legal and court commentary at 2.5x growth with higher ad rates, audience US adults 25-54.
riskNote: Expert commentary is transformative; avoid AI 'lawyer' personas, which the July 2026 clarification explicitly demonetizes.

examples.note: lawyer breakdowns of cases and pop culture

name: Ranked countdown (Top N)
summary: N items ranked from least to most impressive, with the number one held back until the end.

structure.what: Tease number one without naming it.
Quick entries, each with a fact and visual.
The payoff with the best footage.

titlePatterns: Ranking Every [Thing] From Worst to Best
hookTemplates: Number one on this list shouldn't exist.
We ranked [N] [things]. You'll argue about number three.
thumbnailPattern: The #1 item with a large number badge and a reaction element.
retentionTips: Use honorable mentions as a mid-roll bridge.
Put a disputable pick near the top to drive comments.
Avoid identical structure across every upload.
trendNote: Still common, but generic stock-footage countdowns are the textbook 'generic or repetitive' template and slideshow content called out in the July 2026 clarification.
riskNote: Stock clips plus TTS lists are prime inauthentic-content targets; on-camera or deeply researched versions are fine.

name: Tier list
summary: A host places items into S-to-D tiers on screen, defending each pick.

structure.what: Show the empty tier board and a controversial S-tier pick.
Item by item with reasons and banter.
Full board; ask viewers for theirs.

titlePatterns: I Ranked Every [Thing] So You Don't Have To
hookTemplates: This is going to make a lot of people angry.
Only one [thing] is S tier.
thumbnailPattern: Colored tier board, host face, one item in S tier.
retentionTips: Personality is the product; tier lists without opinions die.
Bring a guest who disagrees.
Pin the community tier list.
trendNote: YouTube Culture & Trends counted over 1 billion views on 'tier list' titled videos in H1 2025; format spans 30-second Shorts to three-hour deep dives.
riskNote: Opinion-driven and on camera.

examples.note: commentary creator who regularly does tier lists (verify specific uploads)

name: Price-tier versus ($1 vs $1,000)
summary: The same thing at escalating price or effort tiers, compared head to head.

structure.what: Show the most expensive tier first.
Mid tier, the surprise winner setup.

hookTemplates: One of these cost $1. One cost $10,000. You can't tell which.
I spent [amount] to find out if expensive [thing] is a scam.
thumbnailPattern: Side-by-side items with price tags in bold contrast.
retentionTips: Escalate visibly; each tier should look different.
Give a clear verdict.
Paddy Galloway: transplant proven formats into new niches.
trendNote: Paddy Galloway (Colin & Samir, 2026) cites '$1 vs $100' and '10 minutes vs 24 hours' as formats that transplant across niches.
riskNote: Original filmed content.

name: History for sleep (multi-hour narration)
summary: A calm, slow, multi-hour narration about a historical period, designed to fall asleep to.

structure.what: Gentle greeting, permission to drift off.
Chapters of everyday-life history at an even pace.
Quieter delivery, longer pauses, music swells down.

titlePatterns: [N] Hours of [Topic] to Fall Asleep To
Fall Asleep to [Era] Life | Calm History
hookTemplates: Get comfortable. Tonight we're going to [place] in [year].
Let your eyes close. We'll begin slowly.
thumbnailPattern: Dim, painterly period scene with soft text and a moon or candle.
retentionTips: No sudden sounds or mid-roll stings.
Even, low pacing; no cliffhangers.
Longer versions pile up total watch time.
trendNote: OutlierKit tracks sleep and ambient content at 14x year-over-year growth with low competition; TV now over half of US watch time, and long passive viewing fits living rooms.
riskNote: The niche is flooded with templated AI narration; original scripts and a recurring human or distinctive voice are what keep channels monetized.

name: Ambient soundscape and lofi stream
summary: Hours of looping visuals and music or room sounds for study, work or sleep.

structure.what: Establish the space (rainy window, cabin, spaceship).
Seamless visual loop and evolving audio.
Small changes (a cat moves, thunder) to reward glances.
Chat, timers, song IDs when streamed.

hookTemplates: (No voice: first frame is the scene)
Put this on and get some work done.
thumbnailPattern: A cozy illustrated or filmed space with warm light, small title.
retentionTips: Original or licensed music only.
Distinct world-building beats generic stock loops.
Live versions build community.
trendNote: Strong TV fit, but identical uploads are what the 'repetitive' language targets; growth concentrates in branded worlds.
riskNote: Near-identical loops uploaded at volume are a classic repetitive-content pattern.

examples.note: 24/7 lofi radio with a recurring character

name: ASMR and sleep roleplay
summary: Whispered, tactile sound roleplays designed to relax or trigger tingles.
hookTemplates: Hi, come in, sit down. I'm going to take care of you tonight.
If you can't sleep, try this.
thumbnailPattern: Close-up of the creator with a trigger object, soft lighting.
retentionTips: Keep external links clean; in August 2026 YouTube terminated ASMR channels for links to sexual content.
Recurring characters and series.
Offer a no-talking version.

name: Reddit story over gameplay
summary: A narrated Reddit post with captions over Minecraft parkour or Subway Surfers footage.

structure.what: Post title as a caption and line one of narration.

hookTemplates: AITA for refusing to [action] at my sister's wedding?
My boss fired me by text. Big mistake.
thumbnailPattern: Shorts frame: bold caption over gameplay; no custom thumbnail needed.
retentionTips: Add your own reaction or verdict on screen.
Use Shorts series for multi-part stories.
Rewrite posts; don't read verbatim.

examples.note: curated Reddit drama with editorial voice

name: 3D animated 'how it works' fact Short
summary: A 30-60 second 3D-animated answer to one weird or gross question about the body, history or survival.

structure.what: Visual question ('What happens if you swallow gum?').
End that cuts back to the opening frame.

hookTemplates: This is what happens inside your body when you [action].
Doctors had to remove [N] [things] from this man.
thumbnailPattern: Shorts first frame shows the impossible inside view.
retentionTips: First frame must be the most visual moment.
Seamless loop to drive replays.
Consistent 3D character style across uploads.

name: Non-verbal family skit Short
summary: A wordless, Tom-and-Jerry-style physical comedy skit that works in any language.

structure.what: A tempting object and two characters.
One tries to trick the other.
Final twist, often a third character.

hookTemplates: (No dialogue: the object and a sneaky look)
thumbnailPattern: Expressive face plus the prop; emojis in title instead of text.
retentionTips: No dialogue means global reach without dubbing.
Exaggerated expressions and sound effects.
Recurring characters.
trendNote: Non-verbal Shorts built some of 2025-26's biggest channels: KL BRO Biju Rithvik (80M+ subscribers, India) and South Korea's KIMPRO (130M+, world's most-viewed monthly channel in Jan 2025).

name: Street interview Short
summary: A host stops strangers with one question (salary, opinion, quiz) and cuts the best answers.
titlePatterns: How Much Do You Make as a [Job]?
hookTemplates: What do you do and how much do you make?
Quick question: [question]?
thumbnailPattern: Mic in frame, respondent mid-answer, caption of the answer.
retentionTips: Lead with the best answer.
Consistent mic and caption branding.
Get releases; likeness and privacy complaints are rising.
trendNote: Salary Transparent Street was acquired by NowThis in January 2026; brands now copy the format for ads.
riskNote: Original footage.

name: Podcast clip Short
summary: The single most quotable 30-60 seconds of a long podcast episode, captioned and reframed vertical.

structure.what: Start mid-sentence on the boldest claim.

hookTemplates: The biggest mistake people make with [topic] is...
I've never said this publicly, but...
thumbnailPattern: Tight vertical crop on the speaker with big burned-in captions.
retentionTips: One complete idea per clip.
Add a visual hook, not a lazy crop.
Link to the full episode via related video.

examples.note: heavy clip program off long episodes

name: Satisfying process and restoration
summary: Watching something get made, cleaned or restored from start to finish with crisp sound and no talking.

structure.what: The worst-looking state or raw material.

titlePatterns: How [Product] Is Made in a [Country] Factory
hookTemplates: (No voice: the rusted object hits the bench)
thumbnailPattern: Before/after split of the object.
retentionTips: Record clean ambient audio.
Before/after must be dramatic.
Long-form versions suit TV.

riskNote: Own footage is safe; compilations of factory footage you didn't shoot are reused content.

name: 90-second mini-documentary Short
summary: A complete story (a person, event or product) told in 60-180 seconds now that Shorts can run three minutes.
hookTemplates: In 1962, one man [action] and nobody noticed for [N] years.
This [thing] was worth [amount]. Then [event].
thumbnailPattern: Use the new Shorts custom thumbnail: archival photo plus four-word caption.
retentionTips: Completion rate decides reach; cut every redundant line.
Group into a Shorts series for binging.
Use it as a trailer for the long version.
trendNote: Since Shorts allow 3 minutes, 60-90 s is reported as the sweet spot in many niches (Miraflow, Apr 2026); YouTube added custom Shorts thumbnails (July 2026) and Shorts series (Sept 2026).

name: Live-action microdrama Shorts series
summary: A scripted vertical drama told in one- to three-minute episodes with a cliffhanger each time.

structure.what: One-line reminder of the last episode.
Freeze on the twist; next episode prompt.

titlePatterns: She Didn't Know He Was a [Secret Identity] (Part [N])
hookTemplates: You married me for my money? Then you won't mind this.
Previously: she found the second phone.
thumbnailPattern: Use Shorts series custom thumbnails: lead couple, high emotion, episode number.
retentionTips: Organize into Shorts series seasons for sequential play.
End every episode on an unresolved line.
Design for TV too; microdrama TV viewing is up 90%.

name: Movie recap explained

This family moves into a house where [rule].

name: AI-generated microdrama series
summary: An episodic vertical soap opera (often anthropomorphic fruit, animals or objects) made with AI video and voices.

hookTemplates: Strawberry just found out Banana kissed Mango.

name: AI time-traveller POV vlog
summary: An AI-generated selfie-vlogger walks through a historical moment ('POV: you wake up in 1351').

structure.what: Vlogger talks to camera in period setting.
Three quick scenes: food, street, danger.

hookTemplates: Okay guys, it's 1347 and nobody here washes their hands.
Day one in Pompeii. The mountain is smoking but everyone says it's fine.
thumbnailPattern: First frame: modern-style selfie face in a period setting.
retentionTips: Fact-check; historians publicly criticized inaccuracies.
Add an on-screen 'fact or AI' note.
Build one recurring vlogger character.
trendNote: Started on TikTok (@timetravellerpov, Jan 2025) with 20M-view episodes and spread to Shorts; The Guardian covered the trend in May 2026, along with accuracy pushback.
riskNote: Easy to mass-produce; templated AI clips risk inauthentic-content demonetization and mislabeled realism needs AI disclosure.

name: Brainrot character animation and lore

Tung tung tung...
thumbnailPattern: Two meme characters face-off with saturated colors.
retentionTips: Layer references; YouTube calls this 'creative maximalism'.
Original animation or lore beats raw AI clips.
Ride memes fast; they burn out.
trendNote: Italian brainrot peaked in 2025 (YouTube trend coverage and Epidemic's 2026 predictions); Kapwing found about a third of Shorts served to a fresh account qualified as brainrot.

Show effort; 2026 audiences reward visible struggle.
